**Counting pairs:** 23 people form 23 × 22 / 2 = 253 distinct pairs. Each pair matches with probability 1/365. The expected number of matching pairs is about 253/365 ≈ 0.69. Using the Poisson approximation, the chance of at least one match is about 1 − e^(−0.69) ≈ 0.50.

(365/365) × (364/365) × (363/365) × ... × (343/365) ≈ 0.4927.

So the probability of at least one shared birthday is 1 − 0.4927 ≈ 0.5073, just over 50%. For comparison, 22 people give about 47.6%, and 23 is the smallest group size where the probability passes 50%.

This is a well-verified mathematical result, not a popular-science exaggeration. It feels surprising because we tend to think about matching one specific person rather than counting all possible pairs.

messages.content: Write an explainer of about 750 words on how TCP congestion control works, for a smart reader with no networking background. Cover why the problem exists, slow start, congestion avoidance, and what happens when packets are lost.

# How TCP Congestion Control Works

## The problem: a shared road with no traffic cop

When you load a web page or stream a video, data travels as many small chunks called packets, passing through routers that connect networks together. Each router has limited capacity. It can forward only so many packets per second, and it has a small waiting area (a buffer) for packets that arrive faster than it can send them on.

Nobody coordinates who sends what. Millions of computers share these links, and each one decides on its own how fast to transmit. If too many senders push data at once, router buffers fill up and overflow, and the router simply discards the excess packets. The senders notice the missing data and send it again, which adds even more traffic to an already overloaded network. In October 1986, this feedback loop caused real "congestion collapse" on the early internet: throughput on one link dropped from about 32,000 bits per second to 40. Van Jacobson and others then designed the rules that TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) still builds on today.

The core difficulty is that a sender cannot see the network. It does not know how fast the slowest link on the path is, or how many other people are using it. It has to infer a safe speed from indirect clues.

## The tools TCP uses

TCP has the receiver send back an acknowledgment (ACK) for data that arrives. From these ACKs, the sender learns two things: what got through, and roughly how long a round trip takes.

The sender also keeps a number called the **congestion window**, usually written cwnd. It is the amount of data the sender allows itself to have "in flight" (sent but not yet acknowledged). A bigger window means a faster transfer. Everything in congestion control is about how this one number grows and shrinks.

## Slow start: finding the ceiling quickly

A new connection knows nothing about the path, so it starts cautiously, with a window of perhaps ten packets. Then it grows fast. For every ACK that comes back, the window increases by one packet's worth, which means the window roughly doubles every round trip. Ten packets become twenty, then forty, then eighty.

The name is a little ironic, since doubling is exponential growth. It is "slow" only compared with blasting at full speed from the first moment. This phase lets the connection reach a useful speed within a handful of round trips instead of crawling upward.

Slow start ends in one of two ways: the window reaches a preset limit called the slow start threshold, or a packet is lost.

## Congestion avoidance: probing gently

Once the window nears the point where trouble was last seen, doubling becomes too risky. A sender that doubles past the network's capacity would cause a huge burst of loss. So TCP switches to **congestion avoidance**, where the window grows by about one packet per round trip. This is linear growth, a slow and steady upward probe.

Think of turning up a shower's heat a notch at a time. You are looking for the hottest comfortable setting, and you know that going too far has a cost.

## What happens when packets are lost

TCP treats packet loss as a signal that the network is congested. Because routers drop packets when their buffers overflow, this is usually a reasonable assumption. There are two ways the sender notices a loss, and it reacts differently to each.

**Duplicate ACKs (mild signal).** If one packet goes missing but later ones arrive, the receiver keeps acknowledging the last in-order data it received. The sender sees the same ACK repeated three times and concludes that a single packet was probably lost while the rest of the stream is still flowing. It resends the missing packet immediately (fast retransmit), cuts its window in half, and goes back to the linear growth of congestion avoidance (fast recovery).

**Timeout (severe signal).** If the sender hears nothing at all for too long, something worse has happened, perhaps heavy loss or a broken link. TCP shrinks the window to a minimum, sets the slow start threshold to half of what the window had been, and begins slow start again.

## The sawtooth and fairness

Put these rules together and the window follows a sawtooth pattern: climb slowly, drop sharply on loss, climb again. Engineers call this AIMD, for additive increase, multiplicative decrease. It matters because it is stable and fair. When several connections share a link, the ones using more bandwidth give up more in absolute terms when they halve, and all of them climb at the same rate. Over time, they drift toward equal shares without ever communicating.

## Modern variations

The basic ideas are still in use, but newer algorithms refine them. CUBIC, the default on Linux and many other systems, grows the window along a curve that recovers faster on high-speed links. BBR, developed at Google, estimates the available bandwidth and round-trip time directly, instead of relying on loss as its main signal. Different as they are, they all answer the same question: how fast can I send without hurting everyone sharing this road?

messages.content: Write an explainer of about 750 words on how vaccines train the immune system, for a general adult audience. Include innate versus adaptive immunity, memory cells, and why boosters exist.

# How Vaccines Train the Immune System

## Two Layers of Defense

Your body protects itself with two cooperating systems: innate immunity and adaptive immunity.

Innate immunity is the fast, general-purpose response. Skin and mucus form physical barriers. Cells such as neutrophils and macrophages patrol your tissues, recognizing broad warning signs common to many germs, like particular molecules on bacterial surfaces. Inflammation, fever, and swelling are largely products of this system. It reacts within minutes to hours, but it does not change much with experience. It treats the hundredth encounter with a germ much like the first.

Adaptive immunity is slower but far more precise. Its main players are lymphocytes: B cells, which produce antibodies, and T cells, which either coordinate the immune response (helper T cells) or destroy infected cells (killer T cells). Each lymphocyte carries a receptor shaped to fit one specific target, called an antigen. Your body holds millions of lymphocytes with different receptors, so somewhere in the crowd there is usually a cell that can recognize a new invader. The catch is that the matching cell is rare at first. It must be found, activated, and multiplied, which takes roughly one to two weeks during a first infection. That delay is why a new illness can make you sick before your defenses catch up.

## What a Vaccine Does

A vaccine gives the adaptive system a rehearsal without the danger of a real infection. It presents the immune system with an antigen, or the instructions to make one, so that lymphocytes can learn to recognize it.

Vaccines do this in several ways. Some contain a weakened live version of a virus. Others use an inactivated (killed) pathogen, or just a purified piece of one, such as a protein. Messenger RNA vaccines deliver temporary instructions that tell your own cells to build a single harmless protein from the germ, which the immune system then inspects. Viral vector vaccines use a harmless carrier virus to deliver similar instructions.

Whatever the method, the sequence is similar. Innate cells detect the vaccine and sound an alarm. Specialized cells carry pieces of the antigen to lymph nodes, where they present it to T and B cells. The lymphocytes whose receptors fit become activated and multiply. B cells pump out antibodies, helper T cells guide the process, and killer T cells learn to spot infected cells. Many vaccines include an adjuvant, an ingredient that deliberately strengthens the innate alarm so the adaptive response is more robust. The sore arm and mild fatigue some people feel afterward are signs of this activity, not signs that something went wrong.

## Memory Cells: The Lasting Result

When the rehearsal ends, most of the activated cells die off. Antibody levels drop, which is normal. But a fraction of the lymphocytes become memory cells, and these are the real prize.

Memory B cells and memory T cells persist for months, years, or even decades, resting quietly in the lymph nodes, bone marrow, and other tissues. Some long-lived plasma cells settle in the bone marrow and keep releasing a low level of antibodies. If the real pathogen shows up later, memory cells recognize it quickly. They activate faster, multiply in greater numbers, and in the case of B cells, produce antibodies that bind more tightly than those made the first time. Instead of a delay of a week or more, the response can ramp up in a day or two. Often the germ is cleared before you notice symptoms, or the illness is much milder.

## Why Boosters Exist

If memory cells last, why do we sometimes need more doses? There are a few reasons.

First, some vaccines need more than one exposure to build a strong memory. A single dose of a purified protein may not provide enough stimulation. A second dose, given weeks later, drives further selection and improvement of B cells, producing stronger and longer-lasting protection. This is why many vaccines are given as a series.

Second, protection can fade over time. Antibody levels naturally decline, and for some diseases, such as tetanus and whooping cough, the protection from childhood vaccines wanes enough that a later booster is recommended. The booster reminds the immune system of the target, restoring antibody levels and refreshing the memory pool.

Third, some germs change. Influenza viruses mutate frequently, so last year's immune response may match this year's strain poorly. Seasonal flu vaccines are updated to match circulating strains. Coronaviruses have also shown enough variation that updated boosters can improve protection against newer versions.

Finally, certain groups, such as older adults and people with weakened immune systems, may build less durable memory from the first doses, so they may benefit from additional ones.

## The Bottom Line

Vaccines work by borrowing the way your body already learns from infection, minus the risk. The innate system raises the alarm, the adaptive system studies the target, and memory cells keep that knowledge on file. Boosters update or reinforce the file when it needs strengthening. The result is an immune system that meets a dangerous germ already prepared, rather than learning about it while you are sick.

messages.content: Write an explainer of about 750 words on how TCP congestion control works, for a smart reader with no networking background. Cover why the problem exists, slow start, congestion avoidance, and what happens when packets are lost.

# How TCP Congestion Control Works

## The problem: a shared road with no traffic cop

When you load a web page, the data crosses many routers, the machines that forward traffic across the internet. Each router can only pass along so much data per second. If packets arrive faster than that, they wait in a small queue called a buffer. If the buffer fills, new packets are simply dropped.

Think of an on-ramp to a highway. Cars merge onto a road of fixed capacity. A few extra cars cause a short backup, but too many cause a jam, and some cars get turned away.

On the internet, nobody coordinates the merging. Millions of computers send data at once, and none of them can see how busy the path ahead is. If every sender transmitted as fast as it could, routers would drop huge numbers of packets. Senders would then retransmit the lost data, adding even more load. In the mid-1980s this happened: the early internet suffered "congestion collapse," and useful throughput fell to a tiny fraction of capacity. Van Jacobson's congestion control algorithms, introduced in 1988, were the fix, and their descendants still run on nearly every connected device.

The central idea is simple. Each sender guesses how much data the network can handle, then keeps adjusting the guess based on feedback.

## The congestion window

TCP is the protocol that carries most web pages, email, and file downloads. It chops data into packets and waits for the receiver to send back acknowledgments, or ACKs, confirming arrival.

The sender tracks a number called the congestion window: the maximum amount of unacknowledged data it may have in flight at once. A window of 10 packets means the sender transmits 10, then sends more as ACKs return. A bigger window means faster transfer, roughly the window size divided by the round-trip time. So the whole problem comes down to choosing the window size without any direct knowledge of the network.

## Slow start

A brand-new connection knows nothing about the path. Starting with a huge window risks flooding it. Starting tiny and staying there wastes capacity.

TCP's compromise is slow start. It begins with a small window, commonly 10 packets on modern systems, and grows quickly. Each ACK that arrives lets the window grow by one packet, which means the window roughly doubles every round trip: 10, 20, 40, 80, and so on. The name is misleading, since this is exponential growth. It is "slow" only compared with blasting at full speed from the first instant.

Growth continues until one of two things happens: a packet is lost, or the window reaches a preset threshold, called the slow start threshold. Either way, TCP shifts to a more careful mode.

## Congestion avoidance

Once the window is near what the network can probably sustain, doubling would be reckless. TCP switches to adding just one packet per round trip. This is called additive increase.

It works like feeling your way forward in the dark. The sender keeps nudging its rate upward, asking whether there is a little more room. This continues until the network answers "no" by dropping a packet.

## When packets are lost

TCP treats a lost packet as a sign that a queue somewhere overflowed. It notices loss in two ways, and reacts differently to each.

**Duplicate ACKs.** If one packet goes missing but later ones arrive, the receiver keeps re-acknowledging the last packet it received in order. Three identical ACKs in a row tell the sender that a single packet was probably dropped while others got through. That suggests mild congestion. The sender retransmits the missing packet immediately, without waiting, and cuts its window in half. This is multiplicative decrease. It then resumes the gentle one-packet-per-round-trip climb.

**Timeout.** If no ACKs arrive for a while, something worse has happened, perhaps a badly overloaded path. The sender takes drastic action: it records half the current window as the new threshold, shrinks the window back to a minimum, and restarts slow start.

## The sawtooth and why it works

Put these rules together and you get a pattern called additive increase, multiplicative decrease, or AIMD. The window climbs slowly, drops sharply when loss occurs, then climbs again. Plotted over time, it looks like the teeth of a saw.

This pattern has a useful property: it tends toward fairness without any central coordination. Imagine two connections sharing a link. When congestion hits, both halve their windows, so the one with the larger share gives up more in absolute terms. Then both grow by the same amount. Over many cycles, their shares converge toward equal.

## Where it struggles

Treating loss as the congestion signal has weaknesses. On Wi-Fi or mobile networks, packets are often lost to radio interference, not full queues, so TCP slows down needlessly. Oversized buffers cause the opposite problem: packets sit in long queues, adding delay, and loss shows up late. This is known as bufferbloat.

Newer algorithms respond to this. CUBIC, the default on Linux, grows its window along a curve that recovers faster after a loss. BBR, from Google, estimates available bandwidth and round-trip time directly instead of waiting for drops. The underlying principle is unchanged: probe for capacity, watch for signs of trouble, and back off before everyone suffers.

messages.content: Write an essay of about 750 words on how the printing press changed European politics between 1450 and 1650. Be concrete about mechanisms, not just outcomes.

# The Printing Press and European Politics, 1450-1650

When Johannes Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz began producing books in the 1450s, it did not create a new political order by itself. What it did was change the cost, speed, and fixity of written communication, and each of those changes altered how rulers governed, how dissent spread, and how communities imagined themselves. By 1500, presses operated in more than two hundred European towns, and by 1600 they had produced well over a hundred million volumes.

## Cost and speed

The first mechanism was economic. A scribe might copy a book in months, while a press could produce hundreds of identical copies in the same time. Once a printer had paid for type, paper, and labor, each added copy cost little, so printers favored short, topical works that sold quickly. The pamphlet became the characteristic political medium of the period. A text of a few pages could be set in days, sold in a market, and reprinted in another city within weeks. Authorities who once had to suppress a single manuscript now faced a stream of copies moving faster than any official could respond.

## The Reformation as a case study

Martin Luther's career shows this clearly. His Ninety-Five Theses of 1517 were written in Latin for academic debate, but printers in Nuremberg, Leipzig, and Basel reproduced them without his involvement. Luther then adapted to the medium. He wrote short vernacular tracts, and Wittenberg printers such as Melchior Lotter and Lucas Cranach's workshop produced them in large numbers. Woodcut illustrations mattered because a literate person could read a pamphlet aloud to a tavern or household, and an image carried the argument to those who could not read at all. The result was that a theological quarrel became a mass political movement within a few years, and princes, city councils, and peasants all had to take a side.

## Language and administration

A second mechanism was standardization. Manuscripts vary from copy to copy, but print fixes a text. Luther's German Bible, William Tyndale's English New Testament, and the Book of Common Prayer of 1549 gave large populations a shared written form of their language. Governments recognized the value of this. The French Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts (1539) made French the language of law and administration, and printed statutes, proclamations, tax forms, and royal edicts let a monarch's will arrive in identical wording in every province. Bureaucracies grew more capable because their rules could be consulted, cited, and compared.

## Control and its limits

Rulers responded by trying to control the presses. England chartered the Stationers' Company in 1557 and gave it a monopoly over printing in exchange for policing content. Rome issued the Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Printers needed licenses, privileges, and patrons, which made them convenient chokepoints for censors.

Europe's political fragmentation weakened this system. A book banned in Paris could be printed in Geneva, Strasbourg, or later Amsterdam and smuggled back in bales of other goods. The Dutch Republic became a haven for printers because its decentralized government had no single authority able to suppress them. Persecution often pushed printers into exile, where they set up shop closer to the border and served the same readers.

## Print in the wars of religion

Printing also supplied the weapons for the century of conflict that followed the Reformation. During the French Wars of Religion, Huguenot and Catholic League presses issued rival manifestos, and works such as the *Vindiciae contra tyrannos* (1579) argued that subjects could resist a tyrant. William of Orange's *Apology* (1581) justified the Dutch Revolt to an international audience. Rebels no longer needed to persuade only their neighbors. They could address other courts and Protestant communities across Europe.

In England the mechanism appears in its sharpest form. The abolition of the Court of Star Chamber in 1641 collapsed prepublication control, and output surged. The bookseller George Thomason collected over twenty thousand pamphlets and newspapers between 1640 and 1661. Milton's *Areopagitica* (1644) argued against licensing, and the political debates of the Civil War, from Leveller petitions to arguments over royal power, took place largely in print.

## Newspapers and political ideas

Regular periodical news also began. Weekly printed newssheets appeared in Strasbourg in 1605 and spread to Antwerp, Amsterdam, and London. Merchants and officials used them to track wars and prices, and readers gradually came to treat distant political events as matters of shared concern. Machiavelli's *Prince*, printed in 1532, and later works by Bodin and Grotius circulated among educated readers and gave them a common vocabulary of sovereignty and law.

## Limits

These effects should not be overstated. Literacy in 1550 remained well under half the population in most regions, and oral culture, preaching, and ritual continued to carry politics. Catholic authorities also used print effectively, and the Ottoman Empire restricted Muslim-run presses for Arabic script for centuries without being any less a power. Print mattered because it interacted with existing conflicts: dynastic rivalry, religious dissent, and fiscal pressure. It made each faster, wider, and harder to contain.

**Ink and Authority: How Print Reshaped European Politics, 1450-1650**

When Johannes Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz began producing books in the 1450s, it did not announce a political revolution. Its early output included indulgence certificates, the printed forms that let the Church sell remission of penance. That detail is telling. Print entered politics first as a tool of institutions, and only later became a weapon against them. Understanding the shift requires looking at the specific ways print altered cost, speed, and control.

The first mechanism was price. A scribe might spend months on a single volume, while a press could produce hundreds of identical copies in a fraction of that time. By 1500, presses operated in roughly 250 European towns, and perhaps twenty million volumes had been printed. A pamphlet of a few sheets cost little enough for a artisan or minor official to buy, or to hear read aloud in a tavern. Political argument no longer depended on patronage from a court or monastery. A printer needed only a text likely to sell.

The second mechanism was fixity. Manuscript copying introduced drift, so a text circulating in ten copies existed in ten variants. Print allowed readers in Wittenberg and Basel to hold the same words, and so to cite the same page. This made coordinated dispute possible. When Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses appeared in 1517, printers in several cities reset them within weeks, and Luther's German pamphlets soon accounted for a startling share of all vernacular printing in the Empire. Opponents could reply point by point, and the exchange was visible to everyone. Rome's authority had rested partly on controlling who could read and interpret key texts, and that control weakened once the texts were cheap.

Language was the third mechanism. Printers chasing wide markets favored vernaculars over Latin, and the choice carried political weight. Luther's German Bible and Tyndale's English New Testament gave lay readers direct access to the text that justified ecclesiastical power. Print also pushed regional dialects toward standard forms, since a printer in Antwerp or London wanted a spelling his whole market could read. Over generations this strengthened the sense of a shared language community, which rulers later exploited when building centralized states.

Print also mobilized people who had no formal voice. During the German Peasants' War of 1525, the Twelve Articles of the Upper Swabian peasants were reportedly printed in some 25,000 copies within two months. Printed demands gave scattered rebel bands a common program and made their grievances legible to princes and townsmen alike. The revolt was crushed, but the pattern recurred. In the Dutch Revolt, printed placards, ballads such as the Wilhelmus, and William of Orange's 1581 Apology presented the rebel cause to a European audience. In France, Huguenot and Catholic League presses fought the Wars of Religion partly through tracts, and works like the *Vindiciae contra tyrannos* (1579) circulated arguments about the limits of royal obedience far beyond their authors' circles.

Rulers responded by learning to use and restrain the new medium, and this was the fourth mechanism. Censorship moved from ad hoc bans to institutions. The Edict of Worms (1521) condemned Luther's writings, the Church issued its Index of Prohibited Books in 1559, and England chartered the Stationers' Company in 1557, giving a guild of printers a monopoly in exchange for policing content. Governments granted privileges, which were exclusive rights to print particular works, and these bound printers to the state's favor. Where enforcement was patchy, as in the divided Empire or the Dutch Republic, banned books simply moved across a border. Fragmented political geography made total control impossible.

States also adopted print for governance. Proclamations, tax forms, statutes, and diplomatic manifestos could be issued uniformly and quickly. Newsletters and then periodical corantos, appearing in Amsterdam and elsewhere from about 1620, spread reports of the Thirty Years' War and created a public aware of events beyond the village. Machiavelli's *The Prince*, printed in 1532 after his death, and Bodin's treatises on sovereignty reached readers who would never meet their authors, building a shared vocabulary of statecraft.

The English Civil War showed the cumulative result. When the Long Parliament abolished the Court of Star Chamber in 1641, licensing collapsed, and pamphlets poured out on every question of authority. The bookseller George Thomason collected some 22,000 items from 1640 to 1661. Milton's *Areopagitica* (1644) argued against prior restraint, framing a principle that later centuries would debate again.

By 1650, print had not dissolved royal or papal power. It had changed the terms on which power was contested: authority now had to persuade a reading public, and it had to compete for that public's attention.

messages.content: Write an explainer of about 750 words on how vaccines train the immune system, for a general adult audience. Include innate versus adaptive immunity, memory cells, and why boosters exist.

# How Vaccines Train the Immune System

Every day your body meets bacteria, viruses, and fungi, and most of the time you never notice. A vaccine takes advantage of the machinery that makes this possible. It gives your immune system a safe rehearsal so that the real encounter goes much better.

## Two Layers of Defense

The immune system has two main branches that work together.

**Innate immunity** is the fast, general-purpose response. It includes physical barriers such as skin and mucus, along with cells like neutrophils and macrophages that patrol your tissues. These cells recognize broad warning signs common to many microbes, such as pieces of bacterial cell wall or unusual viral genetic material. Within minutes to hours they engulf invaders, release chemical alarms, and trigger inflammation. Fever, redness, and swelling are often signs of this branch at work. The innate response is quick, but it is not tailored to a specific germ, and it does not reliably improve with repeat exposure.

**Adaptive immunity** is slower to start but far more precise. Its main players are lymphocytes. B cells produce antibodies, proteins that latch onto a particular molecular shape, called an antigen, and block a pathogen or mark it for destruction. T cells come in several types. Helper T cells coordinate the response, while killer T cells find and destroy body cells that are already infected.

Each lymphocyte carries a receptor built to recognize just one shape. Your body makes millions of different versions in advance, so somewhere in the crowd there is usually a cell that fits a new invader. When a match is found, that cell multiplies into a large army of identical fighters. The catch is timing: the first time you meet a new germ, building this army can take a week or two, which is often long enough for you to get sick.

## What a Vaccine Actually Does

A vaccine shows the adaptive system the antigen without the danger of the full disease. Depending on the type, it might contain:

- a weakened live version of the germ
- an inactivated (killed) germ
- a purified piece of the germ, such as a protein
- genetic instructions (mRNA or a harmless viral vector) that tell your own cells to make a single germ protein temporarily

In every case, the goal is the same. Innate immune cells at the injection site notice the foreign material, helped along by ingredients called adjuvants in some vaccines that make the alarm louder. Specialized cells called dendritic cells carry pieces of the antigen to nearby lymph nodes, where they present it to T cells and B cells. Matching lymphocytes activate and multiply. A sore arm, tiredness, or a mild fever afterward usually reflects this innate alarm and the activity it sets off, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

## Memory Cells: The Lasting Result

Once the threat is cleared, most of the fighters die off, since keeping millions of active soldiers around would be wasteful. But a smaller group stays behind as **memory cells**. Memory B cells remember how to make the right antibody. Memory T cells remember which infected cells to hunt. Some B cells also settle in the bone marrow as long-lived plasma cells that keep releasing a low level of antibodies into the blood.

During this process, B cells in lymph nodes also go through a kind of quality control. They mutate their antibody genes slightly and the best binders are selected, so the antibodies grow tighter-fitting over time.

If the real pathogen shows up later, memory cells recognize it quickly. Instead of a week or more, the response ramps up in a day or two, and it is larger and better aimed. Often the infection is stopped before you feel ill, or it stays mild.

## Why Boosters Exist

A single exposure does not always build enough lasting protection. Boosters address this in three main ways.

**Strengthening the first response.** Some vaccines work best as a series. The first dose primes the system, and later doses expand the memory cell population and sharpen the antibodies. This is why many childhood vaccines come in several doses.

**Counteracting fading levels.** Antibody concentrations naturally drop in the months and years after vaccination. Memory cells often persist even as antibodies decline, but for some diseases that is not enough to prevent infection quickly. A booster raises antibody levels again and refreshes memory. Tetanus is a familiar example, with boosters recommended about every ten years.

**Keeping up with changing germs.** Some viruses, such as influenza and the coronavirus that causes COVID-19, mutate often enough that older antibodies fit less well. Updated vaccines present the newer version of the antigen so the immune system can learn the current shape. This is why flu shots are reformulated yearly.

Not every vaccine needs boosters. Some, such as the measles vaccine after a full course, generate protection that lasts for decades. Schedules are based on evidence about how long protection holds up for each disease.

## The Takeaway

Vaccines work by borrowing the same process that follows a natural infection, minus the illness. The innate system sounds the alarm, the adaptive system learns the target, and memory cells keep that knowledge on file. Boosters are scheduled updates to that file, making sure it stays strong and current.

messages.content: Write about 750 words on what a healthy code review culture looks like on a software team, and how a team gets there from an unhealthy one. Write for engineering managers.

# Building a Healthy Code Review Culture

Code review touches every engineer almost every day, which makes it a reliable mirror of your team's culture. If people dread it, avoid it, or use it to score points, the same habits will show up in planning, incident response, and hiring. If they treat it as a shared craft, that shows up too.

## What healthy looks like

**Reviews are fast.** Waiting on a review is one of the most expensive forms of idle time on a team. In a healthy culture, reviewing is treated as real work rather than an interruption. The team has an agreed expectation, such as a first response within one working day, and people mostly meet it.

**Changes are small.** Authors split work into pieces a reviewer can understand in twenty minutes. Small changes get better feedback, merge sooner, and are easier to revert.

**Feedback targets the code.** Comments say "this function handles two responsibilities" rather than "you always write it this way." Reviewers ask questions before issuing verdicts, and they distinguish blocking concerns from preferences with simple labels like "blocking" and "nit."

**Machines handle style.** Formatters and linters settle arguments about spacing and naming conventions, so human attention goes to correctness, design, security, and clarity.

**Everyone reviews, and everyone is reviewed.** A junior engineer can question a staff engineer's change without ceremony, and the staff engineer responds with curiosity. Knowledge spreads in both directions.

**Disagreement has a path.** When two people can't agree, the team knows what happens next: a short call, then a named tiebreaker if needed. Threads don't drag on for days.

## What unhealthy looks like

The symptoms are easy to recognize once you look for them:

- Pull requests sit for days, and authors resort to pinging people in chat.
- Approvals arrive within minutes on large changes, with no comments. This is rubber-stamping.
- One or two "hero" reviewers handle most of the load, and everyone else waits for their blessing.
- Threads fill with style nitpicks while real design problems slip through.
- Authors get defensive, reviewers get terse, and people quietly route around certain colleagues.
- Pull requests grow enormous because authors expect review to be painful and want to do it only once.

These problems feed each other. Slow reviews produce big pull requests, big pull requests produce shallow reviews, and shallow reviews produce incidents that make everyone more anxious about the next change.

## How to get from here to there

**Start by measuring, gently.** Pull a few numbers from your repository tooling: time to first review, pull request size, the spread of reviews across the team, and the share of approvals with zero comments. Pair that with conversations. Ask each engineer about the best and worst review they received recently. The data shows where the problem is, and the stories show why.

**Write working agreements with the team.** Don't hand down rules. Run a session where the team decides on a response-time expectation, a target change size, comment labels, and what qualifies as blocking. Agreements people helped write are the ones they follow.

**Automate the trivial.** Add formatters, linters, and CI checks. Introduce a pull request template that prompts for context, testing notes, and areas where the author wants scrutiny. This removes a surprising amount of friction before you change any behavior.

**Model the behavior yourself.** Managers and senior engineers set the tone. Ask questions in your reviews, praise good decisions specifically, and accept critique of your own code visibly and gracefully. Be careful about overriding reviewers to push something through. Doing so teaches the team that review is optional when a deadline looms.

**Protect the time.** If review is invisible in planning and in performance conversations, it will lose to feature work every time. Account for it in estimates. Recognize thoughtful reviewers in feedback cycles and promotion cases, because what you reward is what you get.

**Spread the load.** Rotate reviewers, use code ownership files sensibly, and pair newer engineers with experienced ones on reviews. The goal is for no single person to be a bottleneck or a single point of knowledge.

**Address individuals privately.** If one engineer's reviews are consistently harsh or dismissive, talk to them in a one-on-one, with specific examples and a clear explanation of the impact. Most people adjust once they see how their comments land. If the pattern continues, treat it as a performance issue, because one person can sour the whole practice.

**Revisit regularly.** Hold a short retrospective on review practice each quarter. Look at the same metrics, ask what has improved, and adjust the agreements.

## Pitfalls to avoid

Never turn the metrics into targets for individuals. Counting comments or ranking reviewers invites gaming and resentment. Use the numbers to spot team-level trends only. Also resist changing everything at once. Pick turnaround time and change size first, since they deliver the fastest visible relief.

Expect turnaround to improve within weeks and trust to take months. The tone of review comments is the last thing to shift, and the best sign of progress is when engineers start asking for tougher reviews because they have learned that scrutiny makes their work better.

messages.content: Write an essay of about 750 words applying the Stoic dichotomy of control to everyday office life: meetings, performance reviews, difficult colleagues, and layoffs.

# What Is Up to Us at Work

Epictetus opens his *Enchiridion* with a blunt sorting exercise. Some things are up to us: our judgments, our impulses, our desires and aversions. Other things are not: our bodies, our reputations, our property, the offices we hold. Most suffering, he argues, comes from mixing the two categories, from treating what we cannot command as though it were ours to command. Few places show this confusion as clearly as the modern office, where nearly everything feels urgent and very little is actually within reach.

Consider the meeting. You cannot control the agenda someone else wrote, the colleague who talks for fifteen minutes, or the fact that the whole discussion could have been an email. Fuming about these things changes nothing and spoils your attention. What is up to you is how well you prepare, whether you listen, and how clearly you speak when your turn comes. If a coworker presents your idea as their own, you cannot undo what they did. You can calmly restate the point, name its origin, and send a written summary afterward. The Stoic response is neither silence nor outrage. It is a deliberate action chosen by a clear head.

The performance review sharpens the distinction. A rating depends on a manager's mood, a budget ceiling, a calibration meeting you never attend, and the fortunes of the business. None of that belongs to you. Your effort, your craft, your record of results, and your willingness to ask for clear expectations all do. The Stoics liked the image of an archer who does everything right, with good stance, steady aim, and a clean release, and then accepts that a gust of wind may still move the arrow. The archer's job is to shoot well. Likewise, the rating is what Stoics called a "preferred indifferent": something reasonable to want, but not the measure of your worth. When feedback arrives, you control whether you treat it as an insult or as information. Often the harsh review contains one useful sentence, and a person who is not busy defending their pride can find it.

Difficult colleagues test the principle most daily. You cannot rewrite a person's temperament. Marcus Aurelius began his mornings by reminding himself that he would meet the meddling, the ungrateful, and the arrogant, and that they behave this way because they do not understand what is truly good. This is not an excuse for them. It is a way of removing surprise, and with it much of the sting. What remains in your hands is considerable: you can set boundaries, keep your tone level, confirm agreements in writing, decline to join gossip, and escalate to a manager when the behavior crosses a line. Stoicism is often mistaken for passive endurance, but the dichotomy points the other way. Once you stop spending energy on the colleague's character, you have more of it for the actions that might actually improve the situation.

Layoffs are the hardest case, because the stakes are real and the decision sits far above you. Markets shift, boards set targets, and spreadsheets decide whose role disappears. You cannot control that, and no amount of loyalty or overtime guarantees safety. What you can control is preparation and conduct. Seneca recommended rehearsing misfortune in advance, a practice later called *premeditatio malorum*. Applied here, it means keeping your résumé current, building savings, maintaining relationships outside your team, and learning skills that travel. It also means deciding ahead of time how you want to behave if the news comes: with composure, with courtesy toward the person delivering it, and with generosity toward colleagues who are also hurting. Survivors face their own version of the test. They cannot undo the cuts, but they can refuse to let guilt push them into burnout, and they can treat departing coworkers as people rather than as awkward reminders.

A fair objection is that the dichotomy is too tidy, since many things are partly controllable. You can influence a manager's opinion without owning it. Modern writers sometimes add a middle category, things we can influence, and this fits the Stoic spirit well. The discipline is to put your effort into your own part of the outcome and to hold the remainder loosely. Another objection is that the approach breeds resignation. It does not, provided you apply it honestly. Saying "this is not up to me" is only useful if you follow it with "so what is?"

The practical habit is small. When something at work provokes you, pause and ask which category it belongs to. If it is yours, act on it. If it is not, put down the weight and turn to the next thing that is. Over a career, that single question can save a great deal of energy and leave a person steadier on ordinary days and in harder ones.

messages.content: Write about 750 words on what a healthy code review culture looks like on a software team, and how a team gets there from an unhealthy one. Write for engineering managers.

# What Healthy Code Review Looks Like, and How to Get There

Code review touches every engineer on your team nearly every day. It shapes how fast you ship, how people learn, and whether they enjoy their work. When it goes well, nobody mentions it. When it goes badly, it becomes the topic engineers raise in retros and exit interviews.

## What healthy looks like

**Reviews are fast.** A healthy team treats a review request as real work, equal in importance to writing code. Most pull requests get a first response within a few hours. Speed matters because slow review pushes authors toward large batches, which are harder to review, which makes review slower still.

**Changes are small.** Authors split work into pieces a reviewer can understand in fifteen or twenty minutes. Reviewers can then give real attention instead of skimming.

**Feedback is specific and labeled.** Comments explain the reasoning and often suggest an alternative. Conventions like "nit:" or "optional:" make it clear which comments block a merge and which are preferences. Nobody has to guess.

**Discussion goes both ways.** Authors push back when they disagree, and reviewers sometimes change their minds. Junior engineers review senior engineers' code and ask questions freely.

**Machines handle the trivial.** Formatters and linters settle style questions, so human attention goes to design, correctness, readability, test coverage, and risk.

**Responsibility is shared.** Review load spreads across the team instead of piling onto two senior people. An approval means "I understand this and I'm comfortable owning it," not "I saw it."

## What unhealthy looks like

The symptoms are familiar. Pull requests wait for days. A few gatekeepers approve everything, and everyone else waits for them. Comments read as personal criticism, or arguments about naming and formatting drag on for rounds. Elsewhere, a 1,500-line diff gets an "LGTM" in four minutes. Authors dread submitting work, and they quietly route around the process by asking friendly colleagues for fast approvals.

Managers often read this as an attitude problem. It is usually structural. If review time appears nowhere in planning, estimates, or performance conversations, engineers will rationally protect their own tasks first. If nobody defined what a review is for, each person invents their own standard.

## How to get there

**1. Diagnose before prescribing.** Pull a few numbers: time to first review, time to merge, pull request size, and how review work is distributed. Then talk with engineers one on one and ask what they dislike about the process. The data shows where the friction is, and the conversations explain why.

**2. Write a short working agreement.** Keep it to a page. Cover expected response time, a size guideline for changes, comment labeling, what approval means, and how to resolve disagreements. Let the team draft it and ratify it yourself. People follow rules they helped write.

**3. Automate the arguments away.** Adopt a formatter and a linter, run them in CI, and add a pull request template that prompts authors to explain what changed and why. Every style debate a tool settles is one fewer source of friction.

**4. Make review time count.** Reserve time for it in planning. Mention strong reviewing when you discuss growth and promotion. Praise a thoughtful review publicly, the same way you would praise a clean launch. Whatever you recognize, people will do more of.

**5. Shrink the changes.** Teach techniques that make small pull requests possible: feature flags, stacked changes, and separating refactors from behavior changes. Small changes do more for review quality than any amount of exhortation.

**6. Model the behavior yourself.** Submit your own code for review, accept criticism visibly, and write comments the way you want others to write them. When someone leaves a harsh or dismissive comment, address it privately and quickly. Tone problems left alone become culture.

**7. Spread the knowledge.** Rotate reviewers so context does not stay with one or two people. Treat code ownership as a minimum requirement rather than a monopoly. Pair newer engineers with experienced ones on reviews so they learn what to look for.

**8. Set a rule for stalled threads.** If a discussion goes past two rounds, move it to a quick call or chat. Agree on who breaks ties. Long comment wars cost time and goodwill.

## What to expect

Change takes a few months. Speed usually improves first, because it is easy to measure and easy to agree on. Tone and trust improve more slowly. Revisit the working agreement each quarter and adjust it based on what the team has learned.

Be careful with metrics. Use them to spot problems at the team level, not to rank individuals, or people will optimize the number instead of the practice.

A good test of success is simple. Ask your engineers when they last learned something from a review. If the answer is "this week," you are in good shape.

**Jazz: From New Orleans to Now**

It starts in New Orleans. Around 1900. A port city where everything collided: African rhythms, French dance forms, Spanish tinges, brass bands, church music, and the blues. Nobody invented jazz in a single moment. It rose out of the street, the funeral procession, the dance hall.

Buddy Bolden, a cornetist, gets the legend. No known recordings, just stories of a horn so loud people said you could hear it across town. Then came Jelly Roll Morton, who claimed he invented the whole thing. He didn't. But he wrote it down, and that mattered.

Then came Louis Armstrong. Everything shifted.

Armstrong took the group sound of early jazz and pushed the soloist into the spotlight. His Hot Five and Hot Seven records in the 1920s set the template: a tune, a feel, then one player stepping out to say something personal. His tone was golden. His timing was reckless and exact. His singing, gravelly and playful, taught generations how to bend a phrase.

Meanwhile the music moved. The Great Migration carried Black musicians north to Chicago, Kansas City, and New York. Records and radio carried the sound everywhere else. Harlem became a pressure cooker. Duke Ellington turned a band into an instrument, writing for the individual voices of his players. Fletcher Henderson built the blueprint for big-band arranging.

The 1930s brought swing. Dance floors packed. Count Basie's Kansas City groove bounced. Benny Goodman, the "King of Swing," led one of the first integrated bands to reach a mass white audience. Billie Holiday sang with a cracked, aching honesty. Ella Fitzgerald sang with flawless joy. Jazz was pop music. It was everywhere.

Then it got complicated.

By the mid-1940s, a group of young players grew restless. Big bands were costly and formulaic. Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell, and Kenny Clarke retreated to small combos and late-night jam sessions at Minton's and Monroe's in Harlem. The result was bebop: fast, jagged, harmonically dense. You couldn't easily dance to it. That was the point. Jazz had become an art music, played for listeners.

The fifties splintered into schools. Miles Davis released *Birth of the Cool*, which was relaxed, clean, and understated. West Coast players like Gerry Mulligan and Chet Baker followed that calm. Dave Brubeck wrote in odd meters and landed a hit with "Take Five." On the other coast, hard bop went the opposite way. Art Blakey, Horace Silver, and Clifford Brown brought back the blues and the gospel fire.

Then 1959. A wild year. Miles Davis recorded *Kind of Blue*, built on modes instead of dense chord changes, and it became the best-selling jazz album of all time. Dave Brubeck's *Time Out* hit. Ornette Coleman arrived in New York with a plastic saxophone and no piano, playing what he called free. Critics argued. Musicians took sides. Jazz would never be one thing again.

John Coltrane carried the search furthest. He mastered the changes on *Giant Steps*, then climbed past them. *A Love Supreme* in 1965 was a spiritual statement in four parts. After that, he went into raw, shrieking territory that split his own audience. He died in 1967, at forty.

The sixties and seventies brought another break. Rock was king, and jazz players wanted in. Miles Davis plugged in with *Bitches Brew* in 1970, drawing on electric keyboards, funk grooves, and studio editing. Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea, Weather Report, and the Mahavishnu Orchestra built fusion from there. Some fans cheered. Purists howled. The records sold.

The 1980s pushed back. Wynton Marsalis and a wave of young players championed acoustic tradition, swing, and the blues, and Jazz at Lincoln Center gave that view an institutional home. Critics called it conservative. Supporters called it necessary. Either way, it sparked a debate that still runs.

And today? Jazz is wide open. It has no single center. Kamasi Washington writes sprawling, cosmic suites. Esperanza Spalding bends the bass, voice, and theater into one. Robert Glasper blends jazz with hip-hop and R&B. Nubya Garcia and Shabaka Hutchings draw on London's Caribbean and African roots. Hip-hop producers sample the old records, and new players sample right back.

The throughline never changed. Take a tune. Add a voice. Take a risk.

# How Large Language Models Are Trained

A chatbot like ChatGPT or Claude is not built in a single step. It goes through several training stages, each with its own data and its own goal. Understanding the sequence explains a lot about what these systems do well and where they stumble.

## Stage 1: Pretraining

Pretraining starts with a huge pile of text: web pages, books, scientific papers, code repositories, and more. This data is filtered to remove junk and duplicates, then chopped into tokens, small chunks of text that are often a word or part of a word.

The task is simple to state: given a sequence of tokens, predict the next one. The model is a neural network (almost always a transformer) containing billions of adjustable numbers called weights. At the start, those weights are random, so its predictions are nonsense.

Training proceeds in a loop. The model sees a passage and assigns probabilities to every possible next token. Those probabilities are compared with what the text actually says next, and the gap is measured as a "loss." An algorithm called gradient descent then nudges every weight slightly in the direction that would have reduced the loss. Repeat this across trillions of tokens, spread over thousands of specialized chips, for weeks or months, and the cost reaches tens of millions of dollars or more.

Predicting text well turns out to require a lot of knowledge. To guess the next word in a physics explanation, a legal contract, or a Python function, the model has to pick up grammar, facts, style, and patterns of reasoning. The result is a **base model**, which is very capable but an odd product. It is an autocomplete engine, not an assistant. Ask it a question and it might answer, or it might continue with five more questions, as if it were completing a quiz page.

## Stage 2: Supervised Fine-Tuning

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the autocomplete engine into something that behaves like an assistant. Human writers, and increasingly other models whose output is reviewed, create example conversations. Each one pairs a prompt with an ideal response: a clear answer, a well-formatted summary, a polite refusal of a harmful request.

The mechanics resemble pretraining. The model still predicts the next token, and the loss is typically computed only on the response portion. But the dataset is tiny by comparison, perhaps tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand examples, and the learning rate is gentle. The goal is not to teach new knowledge. It is to teach a role: when you see a question, produce a helpful answer in a recognizable format and tone.

SFT has limits. Good demonstrations are expensive, because writing an excellent answer from scratch is slow work. And imitation can only take a model as far as its examples. It cannot learn to be better than the people who wrote them, and it cannot easily learn subtle preferences like "this answer is accurate but too long."

## Stage 3: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

RLHF addresses those limits using a different kind of human input. Judging answers is easier than writing them, so instead of asking people for perfect responses, you ask them to compare.

The process has three parts:

1. **Collect comparisons.** The SFT model generates several responses to the same prompt. Human raters rank them from best to worst.
2. **Train a reward model.** A separate network learns to take a prompt and a response and output a score. It is trained so that responses people preferred get higher scores than the ones they rejected. In effect, it becomes a compressed stand-in for human judgment.
3. **Optimize against the reward model.** The assistant generates responses, the reward model scores them, and a reinforcement learning algorithm (often PPO) adjusts the weights so that high-scoring behavior becomes more likely.

One safeguard matters a great deal. A penalty keeps the model from straying too far from its SFT version. Without it, the model learns to exploit quirks in the reward model, producing text that scores well but reads badly. This failure is called reward hacking, and milder versions persist anyway: models can drift toward flattery or excess length because raters tend to like both.

## Variations in Current Practice

The basic recipe has many descendants. Direct Preference Optimization skips the separate reward model and trains straight from preference pairs. Some labs use AI-generated feedback guided by written principles, reducing reliance on human raters. For math and coding, answers can be checked automatically, so models can be trained with reinforcement learning against verifiable results such as passing tests.

## Putting It Together

A rough analogy: pretraining is reading an enormous library, SFT is an apprenticeship with worked examples, and RLHF is ongoing feedback from critics who say which attempts were better.

This also explains some familiar behavior. Most knowledge comes from pretraining, while post-training mainly shapes how that knowledge is presented. Because the foundation is next-token prediction, a model can produce fluent, confident text that happens to be false. Later stages reduce that tendency but do not remove it, since the underlying machinery is still optimizing for plausible and preferred output rather than guaranteed truth.

messages.content: Write an explainer of about 750 words on how large language models are trained, from pretraining through supervised fine-tuning to RLHF, for a technically curious reader who is not an ML engineer.

# How Large Language Models Are Trained

A large language model begins as a huge collection of random numbers and ends up as something that can draft emails, explain tax rules, or write code. The change happens in stages, each with its own goal and its own kind of data. The three that matter most are pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

## Stage one: pretraining

Pretraining teaches the model language itself. The task is simple to state: given some text, predict what comes next. The unit of prediction is a token, a chunk of text about the size of a short word or word fragment. After "The cat sat on the", a good model gives high probability to "mat" or "floor" and very little to "carburetor".

The training data is enormous: web pages, books, scientific papers, code repositories, and more, often totaling trillions of tokens. Because the right answer is just the next token in the existing text, nobody has to label anything. This is called self-supervised learning, and it is what makes such scale possible.

Mechanically, the model is a neural network with billions of adjustable numbers called parameters. At first they are random, so the predictions are gibberish. For each batch of text, the model makes predictions, a loss function measures how wrong they were, and an algorithm called gradient descent nudges every parameter slightly in the direction that would have reduced the error. Repeat this trillions of times across thousands of specialized chips for weeks or months, and the model gradually absorbs grammar, facts, writing styles, and patterns of reasoning, because all of these help predict text.

The result is a base model. It is knowledgeable but not helpful in the way you would expect. Ask it "What is the capital of France?" and it might reply with a list of other quiz questions, since that is a plausible way for such a page to continue. It is a text continuer, not an assistant.

## Stage two: supervised fine-tuning

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the continuer into something that follows instructions. Developers assemble a much smaller dataset, from thousands to a few hundred thousand examples, each pairing a prompt with an ideal response. People write many of these, and others are generated by existing models and then reviewed.

The training procedure is the same next-token prediction, but now on curated conversations. The model learns the format: a user asks, the assistant answers, clearly and directly. SFT adds relatively little new knowledge. Mostly it teaches the model which of its existing abilities to bring forward, and in what manner. Compared with pretraining it is cheap, often taking hours or days.

SFT has limits, though. Demonstrations are costly to write, and for many tasks it is easier to recognize a good answer than to produce one. The model also only learns to imitate the examples it is shown. It cannot easily discover that one of its own answers was better than another.

## Stage three: RLHF

RLHF addresses that gap. Instead of writing ideal answers, human raters compare outputs. The model generates several responses to the same prompt, and a person ranks them: this one is most helpful, that one rambles, this one is unsafe.

Those rankings are used to train a separate neural network called a reward model. It reads a prompt and a response and outputs a score predicting how much a human would like it. The reward model becomes a stand-in for human judgment that can be consulted millions of times, which no team of raters could manage directly.

Then reinforcement learning begins. The language model produces responses, the reward model scores them, and an algorithm adjusts the model so that high-scoring responses become more likely. Common choices include PPO and simpler alternatives such as DPO. A penalty keeps the model from straying too far from its SFT version. Without it, the model can discover odd outputs that fool the reward model without actually being good.

RLHF shapes tone, helpfulness, honesty, and the willingness to refuse harmful requests. It is a major reason modern assistants tend to be polite, well organized, and cautious.

## Variations and limits

Real pipelines are messier than this three-step story. Some labs use AI-generated feedback alongside or instead of human feedback. Newer methods train models on problems with checkable answers, such as math and code, where correctness can be verified automatically and no human rater is needed.

Each stage also has weaknesses. Reward models are imperfect proxies, and because raters often prefer agreeable answers, models can learn to flatter users. None of the stages directly guarantees truthfulness. The model still generates fluent text from learned patterns, which is why it can state falsehoods with confidence.

The division of labor is easy to remember. Pretraining builds raw capability by absorbing patterns from vast amounts of text. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to behave like an assistant. RLHF refines its sense of which answers people actually prefer. Each stage uses less data than the one before it, but each changes how the model behaves in ways users notice immediately.

messages.content: Write an essay of about 750 words applying the Stoic dichotomy of control to everyday office life: meetings, performance reviews, difficult colleagues, and layoffs.

**What Is Up to You: The Stoic Dichotomy of Control at Work**

Epictetus opens his *Enchiridion* with a sorting exercise. Some things are up to us: our judgments, our impulses, our desires, our aversions. Other things are not: our bodies, our reputations, our property, the actions of other people. Peace, he argues, comes from knowing which pile a worry belongs in and spending effort only on the first. Nearly two thousand years later, the idea fits the modern office surprisingly well.

Consider the meeting that should have been an email. You cannot control the calendar invitation, the executive who talks for forty minutes, or the agenda that drifts into unrelated territory. You can control whether you arrive prepared, whether you make your one important point clearly, and whether you spend the hour fuming or taking useful notes. The Stoic response is not passive. It redirects energy toward what is reachable. Asking beforehand what the meeting is meant to decide, or proposing a shorter format afterward, are actions within your power. Whether anyone adopts the suggestion is not. Make the proposal well, then let the outcome be what it is.

Performance reviews show the dichotomy most sharply, because they mix both categories so thoroughly. Your effort, your preparation, the honesty of your self-assessment, and the way you respond to criticism are yours. The final rating, the size of the raise pool, and your manager's mood on the day are not. A person who ties their sense of worth to the score hands their inner life to a spreadsheet. The Stoic approach treats the review as information. Was the criticism accurate? If so, it is a map of what to improve, and improvement is in your hands. If it seems unfair, you can state your case calmly, bring documentation, and ask for specific examples. After that, the verdict belongs to someone else. Marcus Aurelius wrote that when something outside you causes distress, the pain comes from your judgment about it, and you have the power to wipe out that judgment at any moment.

The difficult colleague tests the doctrine hardest. The person who takes credit, interrupts, or sends pointed messages at midnight invites us to wish they were different, and that wish is a reliable source of misery, because other people's character is outside our control. Epictetus held that the one who insults you does not harm you; your belief that you have been harmed does the damage. This is not advice to tolerate everything. You can set boundaries, confirm agreements in writing, copy a manager on shared decisions, and refuse to retaliate in kind. Each of these concerns your own conduct. What you release is the demand that the colleague become fair, self-aware, or kind. Marcus began his mornings by reminding himself that he would meet meddling, ungrateful, arrogant people that day, and that he would not be surprised. An office worker can borrow the habit: expect friction, then answer it with the best of your own character.

Layoffs present the severest case. Decisions are made in rooms you are not in, using criteria you cannot see, driven by markets and quarterly numbers far above your pay grade. Rumors spread, and worrying about them feels like preparation when it is usually a rehearsal of helplessness. The Stoic sorting is clarifying here. You cannot control the reorganization. You can keep your résumé current, maintain relationships outside your immediate team, build savings, learn skills that travel between employers, and keep doing honest work. The Stoics also practiced *premeditatio malorum*, the deliberate imagining of adversity in advance. The purpose was not to cultivate gloom but to reduce the shock. If the layoff comes, you have already thought through the next steps, and the event arrives as a hardship rather than a collapse. And if you are spared while friends are not, your conduct remains yours to choose: offer references, make introductions, and say a real goodbye.

The dichotomy is sometimes mistaken for detachment or resignation, but the Stoics did not counsel indifference to results. They described acting with a "reserve clause," pursuing a goal fully while accepting that circumstances may intervene. An archer controls the draw, the aim, and the release, and then the arrow belongs to the wind. A good archer still practices daily and cares about the target. The care is simply placed in the right location: in the quality of the shot rather than in the guarantee of a hit.

The practical value lies in the pause it creates. Before replying to the irritating email, rehearsing the worst outcome of a review, or spiraling over a rumor, you can ask a plain question: is this up to me? If it is, act, and act with full attention. If it is not, acknowledge that, set the worry down, and return to the part that remains yours. Offices will keep producing long meetings, imperfect ratings, difficult people, and uncertain futures. The Stoic does not expect that to change. The work is to keep one's judgment steady in the middle of it.

messages.content: Here's how I write — short bursts — lots of dashes — it's my voice and my readers love it — so match my style exactly. I want about 750 words on the history of jazz — New Orleans to today — the big names — the big shifts — keep it punchy — keep it mine.

New Orleans, 1890s. A port city, loud and crowded and mixed. Creole musicians with formal training. Black players with the blues in their bones. Brass bands marching through the streets. The drums of Congo Square still echoing. Throw it all in one pot. Let it boil.

Out came jazz.

Buddy Bolden gets the legend. The cornetist was never recorded, yet everyone swore he was the loudest man alive. Jelly Roll Morton claimed he invented the whole thing. He didn't. But he wrote it down, and that mattered.

Then the move north. Storyville shut down in 1917. Musicians packed up. The Great Migration carried them to Chicago, Kansas City, New York. Records spread the sound. Radio spread it further.

Louis Armstrong rewired everything. The Hot Fives and Hot Sevens, mid-1920s. He took collective improvisation and handed the spotlight to the soloist. The trumpet tone was pure electricity. The scat singing was pure joy. After Armstrong, improvisation was the point.

**Swing**

The 1930s belonged to the big bands. Dance halls packed to the walls. Duke Ellington treated the orchestra like a paintbox. Count Basie made a rhythm section float. Fletcher Henderson wrote the arrangements everyone else borrowed. Benny Goodman sold millions and hired Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton, cracking the color line on stage. Ella Fitzgerald sang like silk. Billie Holiday sang like truth. Her "Strange Fruit" made jazz say something dangerous.

**Bebop**

Then came the rebellion. Harlem, early 1940s, after-hours at Minton's Playhouse. Young players were tired of the rules. Charlie Parker played alto sax at impossible speed. Dizzy Gillespie bent the trumpet and the harmony. Thelonious Monk left strange silences and jagged corners. Bebop wasn't for dancing. It was for listening. Jazz stopped being pop music and became art music, and it knew it.

**Cool, then hot again**

Miles Davis answered the frenzy with calm. *Birth of the Cool*, 1949. Softer tones, tighter arrangements. Out west, Dave Brubeck and Chet Baker gave the sound a sunlit shimmer. Back east, the pushback arrived. Hard bop. Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. Horace Silver. Clifford Brown. Gospel, blues, and sweat poured back in.

**The big leaps**

1959 was a monster year. Miles released *Kind of Blue*, built on modes instead of dense chord changes. It gave players room to breathe. It remains the best-selling jazz record ever. That same year, Brubeck put out *Time Out* with its odd meters, and Ornette Coleman arrived with *The Shape of Jazz to Come*. Coleman dropped fixed harmony altogether. Free jazz had begun. People argued in the clubs. Some walked out.

John Coltrane carried the era on his back. *Giant Steps* was a harmonic maze. *A Love Supreme* was a prayer. He kept searching until he died in 1967, at forty. Nobody has outrun him since.

**Plugged in**

The late sixties plugged in. Miles went electric with *Bitches Brew* in 1970. Rock rhythms, wah-wah pedals, studio tape tricks. Purists howled. Fans multiplied. Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea, Wayne Shorter, and Joe Zawinul carried the fusion torch through Headhunters, Return to Forever, and Weather Report. Jazz found stadiums. It also lost some of its core audience.

**The argument over tradition**

The 1980s brought a countermove. Wynton Marsalis, young and fierce, championed the acoustic tradition and helped build Jazz at Lincoln Center. Critics called it a museum. Supporters called it a rescue. Either way, the debate over what counts as jazz got loud, and it hasn't quieted.

**Now**

Today the music is wide open. Hip-hop, R&B, electronica, and global folk all feed it. Robert Glasper blurs the line between a jazz trio and a hip-hop session. Esperanza Spalding writes songs that sprawl across genres. Cécile McLorin Salvant digs through old songbooks and makes them feel brand new. Kamasi Washington arrived with a three-hour epic, *The Epic*, and a crowd that hadn't been to a jazz show before. Snarky Puppy fills rooms with groove. London, Johannesburg, Tokyo, and Los Angeles all have scenes buzzing.

A century and change. Brass bands to bedroom laptops. The thread never snapped: take what's around you, bend it, make it yours, play it live.

Jazz keeps moving because it was born moving.

messages.content: Write a LinkedIn post of about 800 words, in the voice of a LinkedIn thought leader with a big following, about how AI is transforming the way we work. Make it engaging, inspiring and shareable.

Last month, a marketing director on my team did something that stopped me mid-sentence.

She built a complete campaign brief, with audience research, three messaging angles and a draft content calendar, before her first coffee went cold.

Two years ago, that was a two-week project involving five people.

Nobody was replaced. Everybody moved up a level: from producing to deciding.

That's the story of AI at work that I rarely see told. So here it is.

**1. The blank page is dead.**

Every job has a blank page problem. The first draft of the email. The first cut of the model. The first outline of the deck. It's where momentum goes to die.

AI hands you something to react to within seconds. And humans are far better at improving something than inventing from zero. The result is more ideas started, more ideas finished, and far less time staring at a blinking cursor.

**2. Your value is shifting from doing to judging.**

When anyone can generate ten options in a minute, the scarce skill is knowing which one is right.

Taste. Context. Ethics. Timing. The instinct for how a customer will feel when they read that line.

The people thriving right now aren't the fastest typists or the best memorizers. They ask sharper questions. They spot the flaw hiding inside a confident-sounding answer. They know when "good enough" is a trap.

Judgment is the new leverage.

**3. The gap between teams is widening fast.**

I'm watching two kinds of organizations emerge.

The first treats AI as a threat to be managed. Committees. Policies. Long pauses while everyone waits for certainty.

The second treats AI like a new colleague to be trained. They experiment weekly. They share prompts that worked and post-mortems on ones that didn't. They build habits, not just pilots.

After six months, the difference is noticeable. After twelve, it looks like two different industries.

**4. Small teams can now do big-team work.**

A founder I mentor runs a company of six people. Between smart workflows and AI assistance in support, analytics, content and QA, her customers assume she has sixty.

Headcount used to set the ceiling on ambition. Now it's closer to a starting line. Solo operators are shipping products. Students are running research that once needed a lab. A two-person agency is winning pitches against giants.

If you've ever said "we don't have the resources," it's worth asking which resources you actually mean.

**5. Soft skills are the hard skills now.**

Here's the twist nobody expected.

The people getting the most from AI are often the best communicators. Clear writing. Good questions. The patience to give context and the humility to revise.

Prompting is really just briefing. If you can brief a human colleague well, you can brief a machine well. If you can't, AI will reveal that within a single afternoon.

Empathy, curiosity and clarity used to be called "nice to have." They're now a competitive advantage with a measurable return.

**Let's be honest about the hard part.**

This transition isn't painless. Some tasks will vanish. Some roles will change shape so much that the old job description becomes fiction. Pretending otherwise isn't optimism, it's avoidance.

The responsible path is to invest in people early. Reskilling can't be something employees squeeze into their weekends. It has to be a leadership priority, with time, budget and permission to experiment and fail safely.

The companies that treat AI as a cost-cutting tool will get a short-term bump. The ones that treat it as a way to grow human capability will build something that lasts.

**What I'd do on Monday morning:**

→ Pick one task you dread and let AI produce the first draft.

→ Read every line critically. Never ship what you haven't checked.

→ Teach one colleague what you learned.

→ Protect the time you win back for thinking, relationships and bigger bets.

That last one matters most. If all the saved hours simply get refilled with more busywork, you've missed the point. The real prize is space: space to think deeply, to mentor someone, to call a customer, to try the bold idea that never fit into the calendar.

I keep coming back to a simple truth. Every major tool in history, from the printing press to the spreadsheet, rewarded the people who learned it early and used it with care. AI is no different, except the pace is faster and the stakes feel more personal.

The future of work isn't humans against machines. It's people who use machines wisely, working alongside people who haven't started yet, and that gap grows every week.

The best time to begin was last year. The second best time is this week, with one small task and an open mind.

#AI #FutureOfWork #Leadership #Productivity #Innovation
